blocks.title: Differentiate an outer power with an inner function
blocks.prompt:

addmaths-0606-d1-product-rule.description: Differentiate the product of two functions and use the result to find a tangent.

sections.title: Which factor stays unchanged?
sections.label: Keep a factor

blocks.html: Keep one factor in each term, then differentiate the other.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For \(y=uv\), write \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=u^\prime v+uv^\prime\). Label both factors and their derivatives.

blocks.title: Differentiate two changing factors
blocks.prompt:
A curve has equation \(y=\left(x + 2\right)^{2} \left(4 x + 3\right)\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Keep one factor unchanged in each of the two derivative terms.
blocks.solution:
With \(u=\left(x + 2\right)^{2}\) and \(v=4 x + 3\), use \((uv)^\prime=u^\prime v+uv^\prime\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} + \left(2 x + 4\right) \left(4 x + 3\right)\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=4 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} + \left(2 x + 4\right) \left(4 x + 3\right)\).

retry.feedback: A product of derivatives does not account for the changes in the two original factors.

blocks.html: Multiplying the two derivatives alone drops both original factors.

blocks.title: Differentiate two changing factors
blocks.prompt:
A curve has equation \(y=\sqrt{x + 2} \left(x^{2} + x + 6\right)\). Take \(x>-2\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).
blocks.hint: Keep one factor unchanged in each of the two derivative terms.
blocks.solution:
With \(u=x^{2} + x + 6\) and \(v=\sqrt{x + 2}\), use \((uv)^\prime=u^\prime v+uv^\prime\).

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\sqrt{x + 2} \left(2 x + 1\right) + \frac{x^{2} + x + 6}{2 \sqrt{x + 2}}\)

Answer: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\sqrt{x + 2} \left(2 x + 1\right) + \frac{x^{2} + x + 6}{2 \sqrt{x + 2}}\).

retry.feedback: A product of derivatives does not account for the changes in the two original factors.

revision.body:
What fixes a tangent line?

The curve gives the point and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\) gives the tangent's gradient at that point.

How is the normal gradient calculated?

For a non-zero finite tangent gradient m, the perpendicular normal gradient is its negative reciprocal.

What if the tangent is horizontal?

A horizontal tangent has gradient zero. Its perpendicular normal is vertical.

Quick worked example

For the curve \(y=2 x^{3} + 5 x + 9\), consider the point with \(x=1\).

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=1\).

Substitute \(1\) into \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\) after differentiating.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\big|_{x=1}=11\)

blocks.prompt:

Differentiate \(A=\pi r^{2}\) with respect to \(r\), then substitute \(3\).

Answer: \(6 \pi\).

revision.body:
Which variable links the two rates?

If an area depends on radius and radius depends on time, use \(\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\mathrm dA}{\mathrm dr}\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm dt}\).

Why must both rates use the same instant?

Evaluate the geometric derivative at the radius stated for the given rate.

What if two dimensions change together?

Use the fixed relationship between height and radius to make the formula depend on one variable before differentiating.

Quick worked example

A circular patch changes size while staying circular. The radius \(r\) in centimetres changes at \(- \frac{7}{5}\) cm/s at the instant when \(r=9\). The area is \(A=\pi r^{2}\).

At \(r=9\), find the rate of change of area with respect to radius.

Differentiate \(A=\pi r^{2}\) with respect to \(r\), then substitute \(9\).

Answer: \(18 \pi\).
revision.checks:
• A derivative with respect to radius does not yet measure change per second.
  • Do not substitute the radius before differentiating. It varies with time.
revision.examTip: Include area per second or volume per second, and use negative for a decrease.

At a stationary point the tangent is horizontal.

A change from positive to negative gradient gives a local maximum. The opposite change gives a local minimum.
